prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice atomic clocks that reach a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and open atomic spectroscopy to tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock combines a simple physical idea with extreme quantitative control. Katori's magic-wavelength trapping removes the Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping thousands of atoms in the measurement, and Ye's JILA group turned that into the lowest systematic uncertainties ever reached, near 10^-18. Theory and experiment agree at a level where one can see a clock tick differently when it is lifted by a millimetre, which is a vivid way of showing general relativity in an atomic laboratory. The work is not a one-laboratory result: JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others have reproduced and surpassed each other for roughly twenty years, and comparisons between independent clocks now underpin the discussion of redefining the second. It also asks real questions about nature (constant variation, ultralight dark matter, many-body spin physics in a clock) and, as with the laser, the applications will come from a basic capability whose uses we cannot yet foresee. Opening support was the broadest on the list, with all eight members ranking it and all eight naming the same two laureates, which makes the attribution the cleanest of any shortlisted ballot.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier prizes: the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and the 2012 prize for controlling single ions underlie much of what makes lattice clocks possible, and single-ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) compete with lattice clocks at similar uncertainty. A committee could say that this is the maturation of recognised ideas into a better instrument rather than a new discovery. The payoff for fundamental physics is also still prospective, since no variation of constants or dark-matter signal has been seen, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. Finally, I am a theorist who has worked next to this community, so I may overrate how clean the priority story is; Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and others made decisive contributions that two names cannot capture.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as an instrument-driven advance: a roughly hundredfold improvement over the caesium standard, with the magic-wavelength idea being an elegant measurement solution and many independent groups reproducing it.
responses.response: I agree on the substance and on the maturity argument, and I would add that it is the quantitative agreement between independent clocks, not any single record, that makes me comfortable. Where I would qualify Stefan is the instrument framing: if we only say it is a better clock, we invite the objection that the comb and ion prizes already covered it. The citation should therefore stress the lattice scheme, the many-atom regime and what the precision lets us measure, rather than precision as such.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the clocks seventh and ranks the Higgs experiments first. He grants that lattice clocks are the most precise devices built, but doubts the fundamental-physics payoff is realised and sees overlap with the comb and ion-trap prizes.
responses.response: The overlap worry is fair and I take it seriously, but I think it is smaller than it looks. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles and the ion work showed single-particle quantum control; the magic-wavelength lattice is a different idea that allows interrogating a large ensemble without perturbing the transition, and it is what moved the field from ~10^-16 to 10^-18. On the Higgs, I defer to Ulf and Mark on the particle-physics side, and I do not dispute that the discovery is more consequential in the large; my disagreement is that the individual attribution there (four credited names, two collaborations of thousands, the 2013 prize already given) is far less settled than for the clocks, and I would not trade a clean attribution for a more famous topic.

responses.point: Mehlig puts magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, valuing the simple mechanism (band flattening by interference of two lattices) and the clean pairing of Bistritzer-MacDonald theory with the Jarillo-Herrero experiment.
responses.response: I share Bernhard's taste for a simple mechanism, and the flat-band prediction is a very nice piece of theory. My hesitation is about maturity and attribution. The superconducting pairing is still unsettled, and both Eriksson and Olsson note that Yuan Cao and earlier moire theorists (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) fall outside the three names, so the credit is not as clean as the theory-plus-experiment trio suggests. If Bernhard can argue that the flat bands and correlated insulators stand on their own regardless of pairing, I would regard it as the strongest alternative to the clocks in a few years, but I think waiting costs little here.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators first, as a clear, original, quantitatively verified discovery that is distinct from the 2016 prize, while acknowledging that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are outside the credited names.
responses.response: The case is strong and I ranked it fifth only because condensed matter is outside my field, so I defer to Olle on its standing. Kane and Mele's Z2 classification is a real concept, and the HgTe edge transport is a striking confirmation. My concern is the same one Olle flags: the HgTe route was proposed by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and Zhang is deceased, so a trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leaves out the proposal that made the experiment possible. That is a more serious attribution gap than any I see in the clocks. I would keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube neutrino astronomy first, as an instrument-driven opening of a new observational window, with Halzen and Spiering as the leaders, and ranks the lattice clocks fourth.
responses.response: I respect the argument that a km^3 detector in Antarctic ice created a new astronomy. My reservation is that the identified sources are still few (one blazar flare, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) and at modest significance, as Mark himself notes, so the astrophysical picture is still forming, whereas the clock results have been checked repeatedly against each other. I also worry about assigning a thousand-person collaboration to Halzen and Spiering while leaving out earlier pioneers. I would be glad to hear the particle-astrophysics members say how firm they consider the credit boundaries.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will regard lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether single-ion optical clocks should be part of the citation.
Whether two names fairly represent early lattice-clock priority (Katori, Ye, and the contributions of Lemonde and others); I rely on memory rather than a verified record.
Timing relative to the pending redefinition of the second, and whether a fundamental-physics result (constants, dark matter) would strengthen the case if we waited.
I cannot judge the particle-physics, astrophysical and condensed-matter attribution questions for B055, B013 and B018 without colleagues' expertise.
statement.conflict_note: I am a close long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but none of those people are credited on any shortlisted ballot. I work in theoretical atomic physics and know some of the atomic-clock and cold-atom community professionally, but my profile shows no specific collaboration with Katori, Ye or other shortlisted names, so no specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
